Earthdial

Earth as it is right now, seen from any viewpoint you choose; by default, from far above the North Pole. Every clock shown is official local time. Based on xkcd #1335, “Now.”

      Choosing a viewpoint

      Each view is set by the Sun: from the North Pole the Sun is straight up the page, and the other views are turned from that one. Live, the view keeps up with the Sun, so Earth turns beneath it; when you press Play the view freezes to the ground at that moment and the Sun travels around Earth instead. From the North Pole the rim is the equator and only the northern hemisphere shows; from the South Pole Earth turns clockwise. Orbital north and south look down the normal to Earth's orbital plane from either side, where day and night meet along a straight line. From the Sun you see the whole day side. From the Moon you see the face of Earth turned toward it right now; the lit fraction is Earth's phase as seen from the Moon, the complement of the Moon's phase seen from here. Drag to turn the view anywhere in between. On a phone, Compass turns the view with the phone itself: every direction on screen is then the real one, so lying flat it shows Earth from straight above you with north toward true north, and the sunlight comes from where the Sun really is. Set Sun to Stays still to keep the Sun in place during playback too. Clock mode flips the picture left to right: from above the North Pole, where Earth turns anticlockwise, the hours then run clockwise like a clock's. Only the map is reversed; the lighting is still the real lighting of the side facing you. Sundial clock does it the other way: the view turns so the Sun points at the clock's time, the hour marks hold still with 12 at the top, and the map holds still while the Sun goes round it clockwise as the hour hand, just as a shadow does on a northern sundial (which is why clocks run clockwise). The map creeps a few degrees over the year with the equation of time and turns 15° when daylight saving starts or ends. Each preset is a combination of settings; changing the view or the Sun setting leaves it. The hour ring and clock hands appear only over a pole or the orbit's normal, where they read true; the minute strip, marker and hand are left out while playing faster than 1 h/s.

      The shape of the night

      Day and night meet along a great circle facing the Sun. From over the North Pole it projects to half an ellipse with semi-axes 1 and |sin δ|, where δ is the Sun's declination. At the equinoxes it is a straight diameter. In northern winter it bows toward the Sun and the pole sits in darkness; in summer it bows the other way. Pick Loop → Year to watch it swing: that loop steps one whole day at a time at a fixed clock time, so the continents hold still while the seasons change.

      Sizes and distances

      Earth, the Moon and the Sun are drawn to one scale of size (the Moon 0.27 times Earth's width, the Sun 109 times) and their distances to another, shared by both: at 1× every distance is shortened about 41 times, so that the Moon sits just outside the ring. The Sun is then about 570 Earth radii away, far beyond the frame; what reaches the frame is its light, full at its disc and fading with distance from it, so over the few Earth radii shown it is an almost even warm wash, a little brighter on the Sun's side (the marker at the edge shows its direction). Each body sits in its true direction from Earth; when one is nearly in line with your viewpoint it moves in toward the centre and passes behind Earth, or in front of it. The lighting and the Moon's phase use the real directions, and the Moon shows its real face, nodding by up to about 8° each month (libration). Zooming in (pinch, or Ctrl-scroll) magnifies everything together; the maps of Earth and the Moon stay sharp to about 2–3×. Zooming out relaxes the shortening for both distances together: the Moon keeps its place while Earth shrinks, until at about 1/41× every distance is true; further out, the Sun comes into view as a disc a few pixels across with its glow, since from Earth it spans just half a degree. The zoom button's menu has a zoom slider and two other choices: distances always true, or always shortened (zoom far out and the Sun appears as a big glowing ball beside a small Earth). The corner caption says how much distances are shortened. The Sun's surface imitates the Sun in extreme ultraviolet (as NASA's Solar Dynamics Observatory sees it at 304 Å).

      Official time

      The thin borders on land outline the real time zones as currently defined, daylight saving included, and pointing anywhere gives the official time there. The ring shows local solar time: 12 sits on the meridian directly under the Sun, between Earth and the Sun, and each hour mark 15° further east, so the ring turns with the Sun: still when the Sun is still, smoothly when it moves. Clock time differs from solar time by a place's time zone, by daylight saving, and by the equation of time (up to about 16 minutes), so the clock is shown separately: the amber city marker, or the hour hand, sits where the ring reads the clock city's official time, daylight saving included (UTC without a city). It is therefore turned away from the city's own meridian by that difference: about 1 h 15 min for Charlottesville in summer. The UTC mark sits where the ring reads UTC, close to the prime meridian. The outer strip is an ordinary minute dial, 0 at the top and one turn an hour; its white marker shows the minutes of the same clock. Each marker can be turned off under Overlays, and turning off the minute marker removes its strip. Under Clock hands you can draw hands instead (Meridian, Skeleton or Bezel; press H to cycle them): the hour hand points to the clock city's official hour on the ring, and the minute hand is an ordinary one. Above 1 h/s the minute hand is left out, since it would spin several turns a second.

      Inspired by xkcd #1335, “Now” by Randall Munroe (CC BY-NC 2.5); Earthdial is an independent homage and does not reuse its artwork. Surface imagery: NASA Blue Marble (day) and Black Marble (night lights), public domain. Time-zone boundaries: timezone-boundary-builder 2025b, © OpenStreetMap contributors, ODbL. City list: city-timezones (MIT), from Natural Earth populated places. Official times come from your browser's time-zone database. Solar position from the standard low-precision almanac formulas, good to about 0.01°.
